title: Building resilience: how energy prices boost home efficiency
gist: The ECB argues that the 2022 and 2026 energy price spikes triggered a euro area renovation wave in heat pumps, PV and insulation that cushions housing investment even as new-build construction keeps falling, with specialised construction activities at 75% of construction output and works on existing buildings above 60% of housebuilding. Household survey evidence shows high-bill, fossil-heated homes retrofit most, fossil space heating has fallen 3.5pp to 56% since 2023, and the authors conclude this structurally lowers the pass-through of oil price swings to inflation.

themes.theme: Renovation, not new-build, is carrying euro area construction

insights.claim: Specialised construction activities (finishing and installation work) make up 75% of euro area construction activity, so renovation demand rather than new housing starts is the dominant swing factor for construction output.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Construction-exposed equities and building-materials names should be modelled off renovation volumes rather than housing starts.
insights.quote: In fact, SCAs represent 75% of construction activity.
insights.locator: Renovation wave drives building production

insights.claim: Industry surveys (Architects' Council of Europe, FIEC, EUROCONSTRUCT) put works on existing buildings at above 60% of total euro area housebuilding activity, and electrical, plumbing, heating and air conditioning installations alone at 40% of value added in the five largest euro area countries in 2023.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: HVAC and electrical installation businesses are the largest single value-added pool in the construction chain, a direct read on the renovation cycle.
insights.quote: Electrical, plumbing, heating and air conditioning installations alone accounted for 40% of value added in the five largest euro area countries in 2023.
insights.locator: Renovation wave drives building production

insights.claim: Renovations of existing buildings have been the main driver of the recovery in euro area construction activity while construction of new buildings continues to decline.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A construction recovery that is renovation-led means volumes recover without the mortgage-rate-sensitive new-build channel reviving.
insights.quote: Recently, renovations of existing buildings have been a main driver of the recovery in construction activity.
insights.locator: Renovation wave drives building production

insights.claim: Producer prices for the manufacture of articles of concrete, cement and plaster rose 18% in 2022 and a further 7% up to Q2 2026, a cost shock the ECB flags as a likely reason new-build construction keeps falling.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Energy-intensive materials producers are getting price but losing volume; input-cost pass-through is suppressing new-build demand.
insights.quote: Producer prices in the sector “manufacture of articles of concrete, cement and plaster” increased by 18% in 2022 and by another 7% up to the second quarter of 2026.
insights.locator: Producer prices in the sector

insights.claim: Energy price shocks hit construction through two opposing channels: they raise building and maintenance costs and tighten mortgage conditions, but simultaneously trigger a renovation wave that cushions the net hit to housing investment.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The net construction drag from an energy shock is smaller than the new-build drag alone, so bearish construction calls off an oil spike can be too aggressive.
insights.quote: So while energy shocks may slow new construction, they can simultaneously drive a wave of renovation activity.

themes.theme: Solar import boom and the collapse in PV module prices

insights.claim: Euro area PV imports from China nearly doubled after the 2022 energy price hike caused by the war in Ukraine and have remained high since.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Solar installation demand in Europe looks structurally step-changed rather than a one-off spike, supportive for installers and connection equipment.
insights.quote: PV imports from China nearly doubled after the energy price hike and have remained high since then
insights.locator: In 2022 PV imports to the euro area increased sharply

insights.claim: China supplied 97% of euro area photovoltaic module and panel imports by volume and 95% by value in 2025, an almost total single-country dependency in the equipment underpinning Europe's energy-efficiency push.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Any tariff, export control or shipping disruption on Chinese PV would immediately re-price Europe's renovation and decarbonisation cost curve.
insights.quote: Its import share stood at 97% or 95% in 2025 in terms of volumes and value, respectively.
insights.locator: Notes: Concerning panel a) China is the main supplier

insights.claim: The average price of an imported tonne of PV modules or panels fell by two-thirds, from nearly EUR 5,000 in 2023 to only EUR 1,700 in 2026.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Deflating hardware costs mean solar adoption keeps accelerating even without richer subsidies: bullish volumes, brutal for module manufacturer margins.
insights.quote: The average price of an imported tonne of PV modules or panels fell by two-thirds – from nearly €5,000 in 2023 to only €1,700 in 2026.
insights.locator: The decline in their prices since 2023

insights.claim: Demand for efficiency-enhancing equipment spills beyond installation into the manufacturers of the equipment and materials, their upstream suppliers, and the planning, installation and maintenance services around them.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The renovation trade is broader than solar hardware: upstream materials and downstream service providers capture the multiplier.
insights.locator: The increased demand for efficiency-enhancing equipment also supports output

themes.theme: Middle East war spike already showing in subsidy queues

insights.claim: In Germany, 64,000 households and businesses applied for funding to renovate their building envelope between March and May 2026, 16% more than a year earlier, while funding requests for heating investments rose by as much as 40%.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A high-frequency, near-real-time proxy for European renovation demand, with heating-system applications inflecting far faster than envelope work.
insights.quote: Funding requests for heating investments increased by as much as 40% (Chart 2, panel b).
insights.locator: In Germany, 64,000 households and businesses sought funding

insights.claim: Since the start of the war in the Middle East, national subsidy programmes for energy-saving measures in countries including the Netherlands and the United Kingdom have seen additional demand for financing.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Fiscal support for retrofits is scaling with the energy shock, adding a policy-funded floor under renovation volumes.
insights.locator: More recently, since the beginning of the war in the Middle East

insights.claim: The ECB expects a further increase in renovation interest to drive housing investment going forward, because its February 2026 household survey data were collected before the Middle East war and the associated energy price spike.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The surveyed renovation-planning share is a floor, not a peak: expect upward revisions to European renovation volume forecasts.
insights.quote: These data were collected before the war in the Middle East had started and the associated energy price spike. So we might see an additional increase in interest in renovations driving housing investment going forward.
insights.locator: These data were collected before the war

themes.theme: Household triggers: utility bills and fossil heating drive retrofits

insights.claim: ECB Consumer Expectations Survey data show that when household utility costs grow faster in the preceding heating season, the share of energy-renovated dwellings rises, and that share jumped by 10 percentage points between February 2023 and February 2024 just after the Ukraine war energy shock.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Retrofit demand lags the energy bill by roughly one heating season, giving a usable lead indicator for installers' order books.
insights.quote: In the period closest to the Ukraine war, between February 2023 and 2024, this share jumped by 10 percentage points.
insights.locator: Who renovates more?

insights.claim: Controlling for ownership, property type, age, past renovations and region, a EUR 100 increase in monthly utility costs is associated with a 0.8 percentage point higher probability of planning an energy-efficiency renovation, oil or gas heating with 1.7 percentage points higher, and renewable heating systems with 4.0 percentage points lower.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Quantifies the retrofit elasticity: the addressable market is concentrated in high-bill, fossil-heated homes, which is where installers and lenders should target.
insights.quote: A €100 increase in monthly utility costs is related to a 0.8 percentage point higher renovation probability, a 1.7 percentage point higher probability of using oil or gas heating and a 4.0 percentage point lower probability of relying on renewable heating systems.
insights.locator: Notes: In panel a) the blue line shows

insights.claim: As of February 2026, energy-efficiency renovations were the most frequently mentioned planned renovation type after general repairs, cited by 14.5% of ECB Consumer Expectations Survey respondents.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A concrete size for the 12-month pipeline of European retrofit demand, and the base case for installer and heat-pump volume forecasts.
insights.quote: Such plans were mentioned by 14.5% of CES respondents.
insights.locator: Households facing higher expenditure on utilities

insights.claim: Euro area households already on renewable heating systems such as heat pumps or solar collectors are markedly less likely to plan efficiency renovations because they were not affected by the recent energy price spikes, implying the retrofit market shrinks as electrification proceeds.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The renovation boom is a transition-phase revenue pool with a finite runway: model decay in the addressable base rather than a perpetual annuity.
insights.locator: In contrast, the probability was lower for households

themes.theme: Lower fossil dependence dampens oil's pass-through to inflation

insights.claim: The share of fossil fuels used for space heating in the euro area fell 3.5 percentage points between 2023 and 2026 to 56%, with the countries that were most dependent cutting the most.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Structural demand destruction in European heating oil and gas: a slow bleed in fossil heating fuel volumes.
insights.quote: the share of fossil fuels used for space heating in the euro area declined by 3.5 percentage points between 2023 and 2026 to stand at 56%
insights.locator: Investment increases resilience to energy-price shocks

insights.claim: Euro area households that carried out efficiency renovations saw utility costs grow about 9% in the following heating season in 2024 and 2025, versus about 11% for households that had not renovated.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The measured payoff is real but modest, roughly 2 percentage points of bill-growth relief, which caps unsubsidised payback speed on retrofits.
insights.quote: the average growth in utility costs over the next heating season was on average around 9% for households who implemented efficiency-related renovations and 11% for those that had not
insights.locator: According to CES data, for the years 2024 and 2025

insights.claim: From 2028 the EU Emissions Trading System will cover the building sector, raising the cost of oil and gas and further incentivising a switch away from fossil-based heating systems.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A dated, legislated demand shock: the 2028 ETS extension is a forward catalyst for heat pump and insulation demand and a headwind for heating fuel distributors.
insights.quote: From 2028, the building sector will also be covered by the EU ETS.
insights.locator: Investment increases resilience to energy-price shocks

insights.claim: The European Green Deal's Renovation Wave Strategy targets at least doubling the annual rate of energy renovations by 2030, an explicit policy tailwind behind European retrofit volumes.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Policy-set volume targets underwrite multi-year demand visibility for insulation, window and heating equipment suppliers.
insights.quote: The European Green Deal aims to at least double the annual rate of energy renovations by 2030.
insights.locator: EU policies are aiming to boost this trend

insights.claim: The ECB argues that improved building energy efficiency and lower reliance on oil and gas heating reduce the impact of oil price fluctuations on inflation, implying structurally lower energy pass-through into euro area headline inflation.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: If the oil-to-inflation beta is structurally falling, the ECB's reaction function to future energy spikes should be less hawkish than in 2022, relevant for euro rates and inflation swaps.
insights.quote: This has positive implications for monetary policy – both improved energy efficiency and lower reliance on oil and gas heating reduce the impact of oil price fluctuations on inflation.
insights.locator: This has positive implications for monetary policy
